articles.headline: Cut Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced Epilogue Seemingly Teases Assassin’s Creed 3 Prequel
keyFacts: A dataminer known as Sliderv2 uncovered a scrapped cutscene in Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced featuring characters Edward Kenway and Miko.
Reddit users and the author noted the dialogue points to a possible Assassin’s Creed III prequel set between 1725 and 1735.
Ubisoft allegedly issued a copyright strike to take down the video containing the leaked cutscene.
body: A dataminer has seemingly uncovered a scrapped, half-finished cutscene buried in Assassinâs Creed Black Flag Resynced, and the specific appearance of a character named Miko more than implies that said cutscene could have served as a teaser for some sort of Assassin’s Creed III prequel.

Unfortunately, you can’t currently watch the video for yourself, as Ubisoft allegedly just issued a copyright strike against it. The scrapped cutscene in question, which was uncovered by Sliderv2, features Edward Kenway walking into a bar and conversing with Miko. For context, Miko is the co-founder of the British Brotherhood of Assassins, which primarily featured in Assassin’s Creed: Syndicate. After Miko states that he âput out a call to the wider Brotherhood,â the scene then cuts to AdÃ©walÃ©.

While the appearance of AdÃ©walÃ© might lead you to assume that this is teasing something related to Assassin’s Creed: Freedom Cry, which was originally included in Assassin’s Creed IV: Black Flagâs season pass in 2013, users on the r/GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit pointed out an interesting discrepancy in the unused cutsceneâs dialogue. Coincidentally, said thread was “removed by Redditâs filters” at the same time as Sliderv2’s video was hit by Ubisoft.

The cutscene opens with Miko telling Edward that âThe king is dead.â Assassinâs Creed Black Flag Resynced ends in 1722, and Freedom Cry begins in 1735âthe same year that Edward canonically dies. This means that the only âKingâ Miko could be referring to here is George I of Great Britain, who died in 1727.
Unfortunately, the video was taken down by Ubisoft itself. pic.twitter.com/Ph64siuPrq
— Sliderv2 (@Totocko97) October 12, 2026

As for why this might imply that Ubisoft is planning some sort of Assassin’s Creed III prequel, that part is simple: Haytham Kenway, Assassin’s Creed IIIâs antagonist and the son of Edward Kenway, was born in 1725.

Coincidentally, the only details we have about Edwardâs life during this 1725-to-1735 period come from the book Assassin’s Creed: Forsaken, which is an in-universe diary of Haythamâs life, and it barely covers the decade between Haythamâs birth and Edwardâs death. This means that itâs free real estate as far as the Assassin’s Creed canon is concerned. Plus, thereâs another interesting wrinkle that ties this altogether: Haytham personally assassinates Miko during Assassin’s Creed IIIâs prologue.

Of course, as much as this all does slot together very neatly, Ubisoft must have cut this for a good reason. As far as I can tell, this cutscene wasnât present in the files for the original 2013 release of Assassin’s Creed IV: Black Flag, which would mean it was created specifically for Assassinâs Creed Black Flag Resyncedâ¦only to ultimately end up being scrapped anyway.

Maybe that implies Ubisoft has altered its plans entirely, or maybe it means this placeholder cutscene was created as a teaser for a future Assassin’s Creed project. For instance, maybe this cutscene was created early, as Ubisoft had Edwardâs voice actor, Matt Ryan, back to record dialogue for Assassinâs Creed Black Flag Resynced. This is just a theory on my part, but perhaps weâll see the finished cutscene in a Resynced version of Assassin’s Creed: Freedom Cry somewhere down the line.

articles.headline: Meta has some Wonder Full new AI models
keyFacts: Meta launched two new AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, for Muse Code subscribers, with Wonder also available via the Meta Model API.
Meta stated that internal benchmark testing shows its new models can rival leading industry models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
Meta plans to eventually power its Muse AI agent with the Wonder models and develop specialized models for all Muse users.
body: Meta is making up for lost time in the AI race. After launching Muse Spark, the first model from its revamped Superintelligence Labs division, and buzzy AI agent Muse, it’s now launching two new models it claims can go toe-to-toe with the industry’s best.
Meta has some Wonder Full new AI models
Meta says the models compete with the industry’s best and will soon power its Muse agent.
The new models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, are available for Muse Code subscribers starting today. Wonder can also be accessed through the Meta Model API, Meta said.

Meta says it eventually plans to power its Muse AI agent with Wonder, starting with subscribers, and will develop specialized models it “can bring to everyone using Muse.” It hasn’t shared specifics or provided a timeline for either.

The company says its new models can rival leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic, including GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1, pointing to results from internal testing on several industry benchmarks. It’s unclear how they stack up against Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, whose capabilities are still coming into focus.

The launches are part of Meta’s aggressive push to reestablish itself as a major force in AI. The company has poured billions into talent and infrastructure and has been steadily expanding its AI lineup, including with image model Muse Image and a heavy focus on bringing useful AI agents to the masses through Muse.

articles.headline: US attorney warns Chinese espionage is 'extremely pervasive,' says Beijing 'playing the long game'
keyFacts: First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli stated that Chinese espionage is extremely pervasive in the U.S. following recent arrests.
Federal authorities arrested Wanying Zhang at a Los Angeles airport for allegedly acting as an unregistered agent for China.
Essayli stated that Zhang conducted surveillance on a relative of Taiwan's president in the U.S. at the direction of Chinese officials.
body: First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said Chinese espionage is "extremely pervasive" in the U.S. following the arrest of an alleged Chinese agent in Los Angeles this month.

Essayli told Fox News Digital in an interview that his office has pressed charges against several alleged Chinese spies in recent months, saying Beijing is brazen in its attempts to build their access inside the U.S.

"I think it's extremely pervasive," Essayli said of Chinese spying. " China is one of our biggest adversaries, and they're committed to advancing their interests. And they're playing the long game, and so they are willing to put a lot of resources into developing sources, recruiting people within the U.S. to advance their interests.
CHINA EXPERT WARNS BEIJING WANTS AMERICANS — NOT THE CCP — TO SPREAD ITS MESSAGE

"They're willing to steal our technology; they're willing to engage in espionage here. So, there's no limit to what China is willing to do. It is a huge, huge concern. We have to be vigilant, and we have to disrupt these operations on our soil," Essayli said. "We have to protect our sovereignty."

"If you look at just the cases we brought this year, just in my office, I mean, you had cases where the woman from Irvine was engaged in espionage against the Taiwanese president's family member . I had a guy last week we arrested, he sold more than $300 million in SI chips, formerly known as AI chips, to China," he continued. "You had a mayor of a local city that we charged for serving as an unregistered agent of China as well, pushing out their propaganda and taking orders from China."
FORMER CALIFORNIA MAYOR ADMITS TO SECRETLY WORKING FOR CHINA, SPREADING BEIJING PROPAGANDA IN US

"So, it's extremely pervasive. It's a huge problem, but the FBI is on it," he said. "They have entire squads dedicated to combating this, and we're committed here at the U.S. Attorney's Office to supporting those investigations and bringing criminal charges to disrupt these operations."

Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine, was arrested earlier this month for allegedly working with an associate to photograph and record the family outside their Seattle-area home, according to a criminal complaint obtained by Fox News Digital.
CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN
Authorities nabbed Zhang, who goes by "Heather" in the U.S., at the Los Angeles airport as she attempted to board a plane to China.
Essayli said FBI Los Angeles agents arrested Zhang on a federal charge of acting as an unregistered agent of the People’s Republic of China.
CALIFORNIA MAYOR ACCUSED OF SECRETLY WORKING FOR CHINA, SPREADING PROPAGANDA WHILE IN OFFICE: FEDS
She allegedly traveled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, videos and license plate information.

"She coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection," Essayli wrote. "She never notified the attorney general she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offense."
GOOGLE ENGINEER STOLE AI SECRETS FOR CHINA, SENATE HEARS IN EXPLOSIVE TESTIMONY
Speaking on "The Big Weekend Show" Sunday, Essayli said Zhang is a naturalized U.S. citizen and confirmed the alleged surveillance targeted a relative of Taiwan’s president.
"She was conducting surveillance on behalf of the Chinese government. She was acting as a foreign agent," Essayli said. "And she was spying on a relative of the president of Taiwan here in the U.S."
The alleged target was Ting-Yu Lai, the U.S.-based son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, CBS News reported , citing law enforcement sources. The complaint does not name him.
"Saw him. Young male. It’s that young one," Zhang allegedly messaged a Chinese government contact while outside the home.
"I am video recording," she allegedly added before sending two license plate numbers.

articles.headline: Burn With Me is a hand-drawn demon card game featuring the artist's own hand - and also, a refreshingly finite alternative to yer Balatro-likes
keyFacts: Burn With Me is a hand-drawn card battler featuring the artist's real hand dealing cards and reacting to wins.
Players act as occult university students placing creature cards around a pentagram to fill a spiritual energy vial using modifiers.
Steam reviews suggest the game lasts around six to eight hours and includes a story across multiple chapters.
body: Burn With Me is a hand-drawn game in which the most prominent non-hand-drawn bit is artist Eva Manuilovich's own right hand. Excellent, no notes. Manuilovich's hand appears on the right throughout each match ritual, dealing cards with a flick of the index finger; when you beat the target score, it gives you a thumbs-up, then reaches languidly towards the card you've won.

The game itself is quite a swish and entertaining card puzzler/battler, going by a quick bash at the demo. It casts you as a series of occult university students, carrying out forbidden sorcery under the eye of a lupine lecturer who is definitely going to get hauled before the PTA, one of these Halloweens. Each level consists of a pentagram. You have to place five creature cards around that pentagram to fill a vial with spiritual energy.

Each card has a base points value, but of course, you'll get nowhere through base points alone. You'll also need to exploit modifiers, beginning with simple adjacency effects: this Ursus card gets a boost if plonked down next to exactly one other card. By contrast, this froggo card gets a boost if it has no neighbours when played, so make sure you play it first.

The possibilities stack up quickly in the demo: I soon had a pufferfish card that inflated and deflated, every time I played it, with its value increasing and decreasing accordingly. I used the pufferfish to win myself an octopus that permanently raised the value of adjacent cards.

It's wise to play your best cards early in the rite, so that you can effectively make use of Burn With Me's headline conceit – the ability to draw a random new card by incinerating a random card in your hand. There's also a sanity vial that allows you to store any excess points from a win, granting you a reserve. All told, while I'm not sure this is a build-crafter on par with Balatro – Steam reviews suggest it'll last you around 6-8 hours or so - it has some decent chemistry. And unlike Balatro, it has a story. Each chapter is a dredging of a particular student's soul, laying bare their sinful desires over around a dozen battles.

Read more on Steam. I do suspect this might leave me wanting a little bit more, but it's nice to get hold of a deckbuilder that doesn't wish to become a lifelong habit. Truly, there is no demon more possessive than a deckbuilder with its eye on audience retention. Anyway, if you like hands and occultism, you should also check out Lucid Blocks.

articles.headline: India's opposition parties march to top court as protests over voter lists escalate
keyFacts: Indian opposition parties marched to the Supreme Court on Monday to protest a voter list revision that removed more than 130 million names.
Protesters and opposition lawmakers alleged the process favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party, while officials denied manipulation and said it removes ineligible names.
Following the march and a weekend crackdown that detained thousands of activists, New Delhi police announced that Jantar Mantar would no longer be a designated rally site.
body: India's opposition parties march to top court as protests over voter lists escalate

NEW DELHI — India's opposition parties marched to the Supreme Court on Monday to protest a purge of voter lists they say favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party, after police detained thousands of activists over the weekend in a sweeping crackdown in New Delhi.
Several opposition lawmakers and thousands of supporters marched through the capital and submitted a petition to the chief justice alleging irregularities in the nationwide revision of voter lists.

Protests led by the "Cockroach" youth movement have intensified since election authorities began the revision last year, removing more than 130 million voters from the lists. The protesters, including opposition parties, are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Critics say the process is politically motivated and risks disenfranchising eligible voters. Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny allegations of manipulation, saying the move is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible names.
Ahead of the march, authorities closed six metro stations in the capital on Monday and warned of traffic disruptions.
Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party described the growing protests as a fight to defend the constitution.
"We will not back down," he told reporters in New Delhi.
Gandhi, scion of India's most influential political dynasty, is seeking to turn the protests into a broader challenge to Modi.

Gandhi briefly rode through the crowd in an open bus, waving a copy of India's Constitution. Thousands of his party supporters, student activists and other protesters followed in tow. The turnout marked a sharp contrast with the weekend, when authorities briefly detained thousands, including leaders of the "Cockroach" movement and journalists, and effectively locked down much of the capital to prevent large-scale protests.
Modi has not publicly commented on the protests, but leaders of his party have dismissed them, with some calling the activists "anarchists."

Meanwhile, New Delhi police announced Monday that Jantar Mantar, a longtime site of mass protests in the capital, would no longer be a designated venue for rallies. Police said three replacement sites had been chosen.
The "Cockroach" movement earlier this year staged a sit-in at Jantar Mantar that lasted for weeks, forcing the resignation of Modi's education minister in July.

articles.headline: Long-lost horror gaming cult classic P.T. gets a much-needed PC port
keyFacts: Coder Lorean Xavier created a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable for Hideo Kojima's discontinued horror game P.T. using original PlayStation 4 files.
Xavier stated the project was inspired by the desire to preserve the game on platforms other than rare consoles with the original download.
Players must obtain a legitimate decrypted copy of the original PlayStation 4 files to generate the playable PC version.
body: For over a decade now, the only "official" way to play Hideo Kojima's cult classic, P.T. —the long-discontinued "playable trailer" for Kojima's canceled "Silent Hills" project —has been via one of the increasingly rare PlayStation 4s that previously downloaded a copy during its monthslong availability window. Now, though, one coder is helping to preserve the game with a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable from the original PS4 files.

Coder Lorean Xavier said he was inspired to work on the "P.T. for PC" project "because P.T. deserved to keep existing somewhere other than on consoles that still have it installed." The open source porting effort rebuilds the P.T. engine in C++ and Vulkan, using the original files from the PS4 game to re-create "every level, model, texture, sound, script and cutscene," according to its GitHub listing. That means players without their own legitimate decrypted copy of the original P.T. will have to track one down in order to generate a playable PC version.

The reliance on real P.T. files makes this port more authentic than previous hobbyist efforts to re-create the look and feel of P.T. for a PC audience. And while PS4 emulators recently reached a point where they could run P.T. completely , this native port also sports extra features, like upscaling and frame-generation, a camera mode, experimental third-person and VR support, and a "museum" section where you can look at and listen to in-game assets (including "unused content").

articles.headline: Sorry, Street Fighter Movie, But Mondo Just Won The Poster Fight
keyFacts: Artist Gian Galang designed a new Street Fighter 2 poster for Mondo depicting the rivalry between Ryu and Sagat.
The nine-color screenprint poster goes on sale for $90 starting on October 16 at 9 AM PT.
The new Street Fighter movie is also scheduled to release in theaters on October 16.
body: The new Street Fighter movie hits theaters in just a few days, and if you're a fan of the Capcom series, you might be tempted to celebrate with some new poster art on your wall. While the official poster for that movie is fine , Mondo's new Street Fighter 2 poster is much better, striking, and it doesn't feature a gallery of floating heads--just one, in fact, being punched off the beefy shoulders of a Shadaloo enforcer. If you're wondering what that piece of fine art looks like, GameSpot can exclusively reveal it for you below. Can you see it? Sure you can!

Designed by artist and painter Gian Galang, this Street Fighter 2 poster captures one of the most iconic moments of the fighting game franchise, highlighting the legendary rivalry between Ryu and Sagat.
The new Street Fighter poster from Mondo
Preorder at Mondo

"Street Fighter 2 was the first video game I ever owned, and it reinforced the bond between art and martial arts that I loved as a kid and has defined my career as an adult," Galang said. "I did my best to create an image worthy of the Street Fighter legacy, depicting the Shoryuken between Ryu and Sagat, exploding with lightning, splitting the composition in two."

For this poster, Galang created a unique, multi-layered composition, and Mondo has reprinted it as a nine-color screenprint on high-quality House White paper. The poster will go on sale starting October 16 at 9 AM PT, and it is priced at $90.

While you'd think Ken Masters is Ryu's ultimate rival, a storied history between the globe-trotting fighter and Sagat has been explored over the years in film, manga, and comic books. In the original Street Fighter lore, their first meeting resulted in Sagat receiving his iconic chest scar from Ryu's Shoryuken, which drove the Thai fighter to join Shadaloo so he could get his rematch.

Street Fighter Alpha changed things by showing that Sagat delivered a one-sided beatdown to Ryu, and in a moment of sportsmanship, he reached out to pick the young warrior up. Unfortunately, Ryu's dark side--the Satsui no Hado--manifested at that point, resulting in him launching a Shoryuken uppercut that left Sagat scarred and beaten. The two would eventually cross paths again, with Sagat picking up the victory over Ryu after his brainwashing at the hands of M. Bison, and since then, they've developed a mutual respect for each other.

In more Street Fighter news, the developers behind the popular fighting game series recently remarked that it was on life support 10 years ago, and the Street Fighter movie is out on October 16. Helmed by Bad Trip director Kitao Sakurai, it features a stacked roster of actors, Easter eggs , and a version of Guile's theme music that goes with everything.

articles.headline: AMD unveils Helion racks for AI agents at OCP summit
keyFacts: AMD unveiled the Helion rack reference design at the Open Compute Project Summit 2026 to run AI agents with CPU-only or mixed CPU and GPU configurations.
AMD SVP Dan McNamara stated that the flexible rack designs adapt to different agentic AI workloads and make efficient use of available power.
AMD plans to contribute the Helion specifications to the Open Compute Project, with partner-built configurations scheduled for November 2026.
body: AMD is expanding its rack-scale AI lineup with a design to run AI agents, offering CPU-only configurations or integrated CPU/GPU deployments, and liquid-cooled or air-cooled versions. Revealed at the Open Compute Project (OCP) Summit 2026 in San Jose, California, the chipmaker's new rack reference design is named Helion, while its existing system carries the moniker Helios, which we can't help feeling is inviting confusion a little. Helion offers an OCP-compliant blueprint for agentic AI infrastructure built around AMD's CPUs and accelerators. AMD launched Helios earlier this year for frontier-scale AI training and large-scale inference. Helion's enterprise configuration instead combines agent execution and inference within a single rack. Customers can opt for a CPU-only hyperscale configuration or an enterprise configuration with a mix of CPU and GPU blades. Depending on configuration, AMD advertises up to 32,768 of AMD's "Zen 6" CPU cores, delivered via compute nodes fitted with 256-core versions of its Venice Epyc processor, up to 16 of its Instinct MI350P GPU accelerators, and up to 102 Tbps of networking bandwidth. The CPU-only hyperscale version offers dedicated capacity for agent execution and connections to separate model inference infrastructure, while the enterprise configuration combines agent execution, GPU inference, and supporting workloads in one rack. Both configurations offer dense, balanced, or high-performance CPU blades. For dense deployments, EPYC 9006 chips rated at 400 W are used, while performance blades sport a version of the chip with just 96 cores but clocked at 5 GHz. Balanced blades use 256-core processors rated at 600 W. There are also GPU inference blades, with eight Instinct MI350P GPUs in a 5U server, plus general-purpose blades, intended for database and storage servers or technical compute workloads. AMD SVP for Compute and Enterprise AI Dan McNamara said agentic AI is not a single workload, spanning enterprise applications and complex workflows, each with different compute requirements. "To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing Epyc performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power," he added. AMD says it plans to contribute the Helion specifications to OCP, making them available to the community for further development and adoption. Partner-built Helion configurations are scheduled for November 2026. In its announcement, AMD cites Cisco, Dell, HPE, Foxconn, Lenovo, Supermicro, and others as on board with the new kit. ®

articles.headline: AI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
keyFacts: UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan warned that a breach of the country's cyber defences is likely.
The government plans to use advanced AI to combat threats and is working with the US to maintain AI model access for the AI Security Institute.
Nuala Polo of the Ada Lovelace Institute stated that the government's announcement committed it to very little.
body: - Published
The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached.
Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June.
He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us".
Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents.
The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems.

He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system."

In his speech, Narayan also confirmed scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), were conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe".
AI testing
AISI began evaluating risks of the latest frontier AI models, prior to their public release, shortly after it was established in November 2023.
But it was reported in September, external that the White House had asked some leading US labs not to share their models with the research organisation until its own tests were completed.
The move was viewed at the time as a blow to AISI - which has been championed by the UK government and its partners for advancing open, constructive and collaborative AI testing.
Microsoft president Brad Smith recently told the BBC the institute had helped cement the UK as the country best-placed to drive forward global regulation.
On Monday, Narayan said that in the last few weeks, the government had worked with the US "to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released".
He also said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported.
Nuala Polo, UK Public Policy Lead at the Ada Lovelace Institute, said the announcement committed the government to "very little".
"Stronger protections will be 'considered', strengthening the Cyber Bill 'explored' and near-miss reporting 'looked at', with the detail to come later," she said.
"There is no new regulatory power, no timetable and no obligation on AI developers."
Regulation
The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems.

On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.
The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown.

However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals.
Speaking to the BBC following the announcement, Narayan said the UK needed "to be confident... as a country" when questioned as to how the government can make foreign AI firms abide by UK rules.

"We have the capability, we have the trust, and we have a government that is right on the side of the British public in making sure we don't just have laws but the ability to enforce those laws," he said.
"What we are focused on is delivering the right outcome for the British public, where the law was the answer."

On the question of whether the UK should have its own sovereign AI frontier model, the minister said he was "focused" on securing British sovereignty, which meant "placing the right set of investments".

"It's British chips being made here. It's British models outside of just language, looking at things like drug discovery, materials discovery, computer vision and its areas of adoption, including AI, security and cyber-security," he said.

articles.headline: I Tested the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max’s Batteries and Was Awestruck by One Change
keyFacts: CNET tested the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and found that they feature larger batteries, a power-efficient A20 Pro chip, and iOS 27 optimizations.
Testing showed that the iPhone 18 Pro Max delivers the longest-lasting battery life of any phone Apple has ever made.
Testing also showed that the iPhone 18 Pro is Apple's fastest-charging phone, supporting 60-watt fast charging.
body: Battery life might be the iPhone 18 Pro’s sleeper feature.

When Apple announced the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the phones were instantly overshadowed by their new sibling, the iPhone Duo, which has a passport-size design with a tiny iPad-like folding screen. That doesn’t mean that Apple’s latest pro phones don’t have their own appeal.

On paper, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max’s marquee features are the new variable aperture and the addition of manual controls in the Camera app, aimed at the niche audience of professional photographers and creative types. But my testing found that the phone’s battery upgrades should appeal to everyone. That’s in part because the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have larger batteries than their 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max counterparts, as revealed in a teardown by the tech repair site iFixIt.

Beyond the increased battery capacity, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have the power-efficient A20 Pro chip and run on iOS 27, which has several behind-the-scenes improvements to reduce power consumption. At a time when companies, including Apple, are raising phone prices – the 18 Pro starts at $1,199 and 18 Pro Max at $1,299 – it’s reassuring to see that the new Pro models are more than just a yearly iteration and improve on the 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max’s fast charging and long battery life.
How do they compare to the iPhone 17, iPhone Air and older iPhone models?

CNET tested the Apple phones’ four ways to find out: a battery stress test, a video streaming battery test, a wired charging test and a wireless charging test. These results, along with our lab data from previous years, show that the iPhone 18 Pro Max has the longest-lasting battery life of any phone Apple has ever made. The smaller iPhone 18 Pro is the fastest-charging iPhone. The performance of both phones in my testing and review is why each has earned a CNET Editors’ Choice Award.
Key takeaways

- Lab testing across video streaming and battery stress tests shows that the 18 Pro Max delivers the longest overall battery life of any iPhone to date, driven by a larger battery capacity and the power-efficient A20 Pro chip and iOS 27.
- The 18 Pro is Apple’s fastest-charging phone, reaching 53% battery in 15 minutes and 82% in 30 minutes.

- Despite being a prior-generation model, the iPhone 16 Plus still holds the best score in the 45-minute multitasking battery stress test, edging out both the 17 Pro Max and 18 Pro Max by 1 percentage point.
The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have an incredible battery life

CNET has two battery benchmark tests (video streaming and stress tests) to rate battery performance. We averaged the scores from both tests for each phone to determine the final ranking. If you’re looking for a phone with the longest battery life between charges, get an iPhone 18 Pro Max, which came out on top.

Because we’ve used these tests for years, we can compare new iPhones against older models. If you have an iPhone 15 or 16, upgrading to an iPhone 17 will get you a noticeably longer battery life out of the box. Keep in mind that display brightness, the strength of your carrier’s signal and how you use your phone all have a tremendous impact on the battery life you get from any phone. If you’re someone who is obsessively online, a phone with an incredible battery life might not be enough for you. Obviously, battery life isn’t the only consideration when shopping for a new phone, and normally, I’d recommend holding onto your phone for 3 to 4 years if possible.

In CNET’s 3-hour video battery test, where we streamed a video over Wi-Fi with the screen at full brightness, the iPhone 18 Pro had the highest remaining charge. What’s notable is how it did compared with the iPhone 17 Pro, which lost 8% more in the same test. That’s quite the improvement in just a single year. The $929 iPhone 17, $270 less than the 18 Pro, might be the most surprising result, placing fourth in the test. It proves you don’t need to buy a $1,300 phone to get great battery life.
The iPhone 18 Pro Max landed second in the 3-hour streaming video test.

In CNET’s 45-minute battery stress test, during which I played games, streamed videos, scrolled social media and took a video call with the screen at half brightness, 2024’s iPhone 16 Plus still holds the best result. The 18 Pro Max and 17 Pro Max placed second, just a single percent behind the 16 Plus. The iPhone 17 lands in the third spot, again an impressive result that shows that the standard model will be more than enough for most people, even a year after it came out. The iPhone 18 Pro placed last in this test, but keep in mind that its result was better than many Android phones, such as the Pixel 11 Pro and Galaxy S26.

Looking at our results, the iPhone 17 Pro Max and 18 Pro Max are nearly identical in battery life, even though the new phone scored a percentage point higher in one test. So if you’re able to get a deal on the 17 Pro Max, Apple stopped selling it, save money, go for it.
The iPhone 18 Pro is the fastest charging iPhone

At some point, you’re going to need to recharge your iPhone’s battery and one discovery I had from testing was just how much Apple improved wired charging on both the new Pro models. We have two charging tests (wired and wireless) to rate recharging performance. As with our battery tests, we averaged the scores from the two tests to determine the final ranking. If you want the fastest-charging Apple phone, then buy an iPhone 18 Pro.

In our 30-minute wired charging test, starting with the battery at 0% and charging with the included cable, the iPhone 18 Pro added 82%, reaching 53% after 15 minutes. Compare that with the iPhone 17 Pro, which saw a 74% increase in the same test. That’s an 8% gain between model years and a wild improvement!

So why the big difference here? The iPhone 17 Pro supports 40-watt fast charging, whereas the iPhone 18 Pro supports 60-watt fast charging. Both require using or purchasing a wall plug that supports those speeds.
The 18 Pro Max added 77% in the same 30-minute test and hit 48% at the 15-minute mark. This is another 8% improvement from last year – the 17 Pro Max gained 69%.
Again, the notable performance came from the iPhone 17, which recharged its battery from empty to 69%, matching the 17 Pro Max.

The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max support 25-watt Qi2.2 wireless charging via MagSafe, like the 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max. In our 30-minute wireless charging test, the 17 Pro beat the new 18 Pro by just a single percent. The 18 Pro Max placed just after the iPhone Air in the same test. Keep in mind that the 18 Pro Max has the largest battery capacity of any iPhone we tested. Though the 17 Pro Max has a large battery, too, it came in third for this test.
The iPhone Duo and final thoughts

Apple will release the iPhone Duo on Oct. 23. We are excited to test its battery and charging capabilities, but at this time, we’ve only had brief hands-on time with the foldable phone at Apple’s event last month.

While battery life and charging speeds are not the primary reasons to choose one iPhone over another, they are among the most important considerations. Out of Apple’s current lineup, the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max will give you the most battery life. But I think most people will be fine with the standard iPhone 17. Think of it as getting the most battery life for your dollar.

The iPhone Air is Apple’s slimmest phone (until the Duo goes on sale), but still has a good battery life despite its petite proportions. And while the iPhone 17E is Apple’s most affordable phone, it has a battery life that beats out most of the older iPhone models that we tested.

Lastly, if the poor battery health on your current iPhone is making you want to upgrade, it’s worth considering a battery replacement. It’ll cost you $50 to $130, depending on which model you have; even less if you replace it yourself. Doing so will add a couple more years to your phone’s longevity and save you hundreds of dollars.

articles.headline: Michael Jordan Last Dance jersey bought for record $14m in private sale
keyFacts: Hunt Auctions announced that a Michael Jordan jersey from the 1998 NBA finals sold for $14m in a private sale.
Real estate investor Ron Firman bought the red jersey, which Jordan wore during Game 2 against the Utah Jazz.
Hunt Auctions said the sale set a new record for the highest price ever paid for basketball memorabilia.
body: A jersey worn by Michael Jordan during the 1998 NBA finals has been sold for $14m, an auction house announced on Monday, in what it said is the highest price ever paid for a piece of basketball memorabilia.

Hunt Auctions said Miami real estate investor Ron Firman had bought the jersey in a private sale. Jordan wore the red jersey in Game 2 of the 1998 finals; he and the Chicago Bulls beat the Utah Jazz that night to even the series at a game apiece. Jordan and the Bulls would go on to win the series in six games, the sixth and final title of his Hall of Fame career. That 1997-98 season was the subject of the Last Dance documentary series, which became a hit on Netflix in 2020.

“While Michael Jordan’s importance within the sports memorabilia marketplace has long been established it has now escalated to an elite asset class more typically reserved for iconic works of art,” said David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions. “We are very pleased to have been able to facilitate this historic sale which serves as another benchmark for our industry.”

The $14m price would be the second-biggest known cost for a game-worn jersey, behind the $24.12m paid in 2024 for one worn by Babe Ruth of the New York Yankees when he hit the “called shot” home run against the Chicago Cubs during the 1932 World Series.

This sale becomes at least the third time a Jordan jersey from that 1998 finals has fetched at least $10m. A jersey from Game 1 was sold at auction for about $10.1m in 2022 and a jersey from Game 3 was auctioned last month for about $12.3m.
“Michael Jordan was an incredibly talented player who is admired around the world.” Firman said in a statement. “I’m very excited about the purchase.”

The jersey was originally bought from the Bulls by a private collector in 2003, Hunt said, adding that it “has remained within a succinct chain of custody having only changed hands once from the original purchaser.”

Jordan’s final season with the Bulls has been the subject of massive interest among collectors. In 2023, a pair of Air Jordan sneakers that he wore in Game 2 against the Jazz was sold by Sotheby’s for $2.2m, touted at the time as “a new world record for the most valuable sneakers ever sold.”

articles.headline: Deadly Saudi airport strikes mark major Mideast escalation
keyFacts: Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis launched multiple strikes on Riyadh's airport over the weekend, killing 13 people and injuring over 300 others.
Riyadh's main international airport remained closed on Monday following the attacks, and several top energy executives dropped out of a local conference.
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he was weighing whether to join Saudi Arabia's military operations against the Houthis.
body: RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — Fears of intensifying conflict were growing in Saudi Arabia on Monday after Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis launched multiple strikes on Riyadh’s airport over the weekend, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds.
“What is clear is we remain on a strong escalation ladder,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at New America, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region.

More than 300 people were injured when the kingdom’s main international airport was attacked Saturday, marking a major escalation in the Houthi rebel group’s campaign against the world’s leading oil exporter and key U.S. ally in the region.

Among the victims were one American, as well as four citizens of Saudi Arabia, two Bangladeshi nationals, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Palestinian, a Syrian and one Sudanese national. The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia later said that an Indian national injured in Saturday’s attack had died.
Video capturing the Saturday attack showed a packed airport before the flash of an explosion sends people running for safety as debris falls on them.
The airport remained shut Monday.
The impact of the attacks were felt at the WPC Energy Congress in the Saudi capital Monday, with several top energy executives dropping off the event’s schedule.

The chief executives of Exxon Mobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected at the event, which started Sunday, but were no longer on the agenda that conference organizers released early Monday, Reuters reported. The energy giants did not immediately respond to requests for comment from NBC News.

“You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said, according to Reuters, as he opened Monday’s session of the gathering held just miles away from Riyadh airport. But, he added, “our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone.”
He said the stepped-up fighting was serious and that the kingdom’s response must be “equally serious.”
“There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix,” he separately said. “We come out of the ashes all the time and every time.”

Fighting on the ground in neighboring Yemen is also intensifying, with the Houthis expanding their operations along its Red Sea coast and around the Bab el Mandeb, a key shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began fighting in 2015 after the kingdom entered Yemen’s civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government.

A period of relative calm following a 2022 ceasefire was shattered in July when the Houthis resumed attacks after accusing Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was attempting to land.

Baron said the latest attacks — the deadliest by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade — could have a “galvanizing effect” on Washington and other international actors, including Pakistan and Turkey, which recently reached a joint defense agreement with the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia defiant following multiple strikes on Riyadh

“As these attacks are growing stronger and stronger, on the one hand, it’s increasing the hurt on the kingdom, but it’s also increasing assessments for many that there has to be some strong effort to degrade the Houthis and restore deterrence,” Baron said.
Washington faces mounting pressure. President Donald Trump on Saturday said he was still weighing whether to join in Saudi Arabia’s military operations against the Houthis.
“We may. We’re gonna look at it,” he told reporters. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

After sweeping gains by Houthi forces in Yemen last month, Trump said the rebel group had contacted the U.S. to stress that it doesn’t “want to fight with us” and would “much prefer not having us involved.”
While the skies over Riyadh were empty Monday after flights in and out of the capital were canceled, roads were full of traffic as residents tried to get back to normal life.
And in the early hours of Sunday, road crossings at the border with the United Arab Emirates were largely deserted.

“With the Houthis, we knew that they could hit Riyadh airport, but it’s almost about the precision,” Baron said. “There’s a great degree of anxiety in terms of ... living in a world where you can just have random armed groups hitting airports.”

articles.headline: Why the right turned on Indian Americans
keyFacts: Freelance journalist Zaid Jilani said that Indian Americans and Indian immigrants have increasingly become targets of online racist attacks on the political right.
Jilani stated that this bigotry is driven by status anxiety and a broader anti-globalization backlash as Indian Americans rise to prominent positions in society.
According to Jilani, many Indian Americans have responded to the mistreatment with pragmatism, acknowledging economic struggles while continuing to pursue success.
body: Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor of Ohio, at a campaign event in Vandalia, Ohio, on October 3, 2026. | Jessica Phelps/Bloomberg via Getty Images

In early October, Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor of Ohio, went for a classic “politician on the stump” move: He picked up a kid. Or at least he tried to. Ramaswamy fumbled the boy a bit , producing a clip that quickly went viral on social media.

The next day, Ramaswamy posted a picture of himself with his son in his arms on social media. It was a cute retort. But many of the responses were ugly — racist attacks against Ramaswamy that drew on anti-Indian stereotypes.
It was the latest example of a broader shift on the right, where Indian Americans and Indian immigrants have become a conspicuous target of online conservative anger.

“The people who had negative stereotypes about Indians in their mind said, ‘Hey, look, the guy can’t even pick up a kid…he can’t even act like a normal American family man,’” freelance journalist Zaid Jilani told Today, Explained co-host Noel King.

Jilani, who recently wrote about the surge in anti-Indian racism for Vox, joined the podcast for a conversation about how he sees the bigotry as rooted in status envy, how Indian Americans and Indian immigrants are responding, and his surprisingly hopeful outlook for the future.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .

American racism is very interesting, always has been. And there is a type that says, immigrants are dirty, they come here, they’re uneducated, they leach off the government, they’re taking our resources.

The stereotype of Indian immigrants to America and Indian Americans is people who go to college, people who often have advanced degrees, people who often live in nice neighborhoods, make good money, are family-values people.
Why do you think these values that seem as if they mesh with what Republicans want are so triggering to people these days? Is it just yes, but they’re brown?

I think that is a component of it. I spoke to one Indian American advocate who told me that Indians and South Asians more broadly are visible minorities, right? If you think about other minorities who are highly successful, that’s not always the case.

For instance, I think that Jewish Americans have been known since the late 20th century as being a successful minority group, but they’re not necessarily highly visible. You can’t always identify someone. If [Texas Railroad Commissioner candidate] Bo French saw a bunch of white people in the stadium with the Longhorns, I’m not sure he would be picking out who’s Protestant, who’s Catholic, who’s Jewish. But with Indian Americans, they are highly visible.

That being said, I think you have to think about where Indian Americans are in society and the kind of feelings that can create among everyone else. If you look, for instance, at Silicon Valley, the major tech companies, Microsoft, Google — the head of [Microsoft’s] Xbox division is an Indian American woman now.

You have a group of people who I think are in many ways a very micro minority — we’re talking about 1 percent to 2 percent of the United States — visibly rising into so many positions that I think a lot of people have typically associated with white folks. White people generally run the Fortune 500, white folks run the universities, white folks are the most successful doctors and engineers. And that was true for the 20th century.

But when you start seeing a much larger influx of Asian immigrants, starting with liberalization of immigration laws in the ’60s, but also when there was a rapid growth of the technology sector in the early 2000s, you start to understand a little bit more where the resentment comes from because it’s more, I would say, analogically similar to antisemitism than it is to the racism that Mexican Americans face or the racism that Black Americans face.
“It’s a much larger anti-globalization backlash on the right, not only when it comes to things like immigration, but also trade and tariffs and restrictions like that.”

It’s not that Indian Americans are necessarily being stereotyped as antisocial, criminal, coming here illegally, so on and so forth. It’s more that they’re being seen as a status threat to a lot of particularly middle-class Americans, people who want their kids to rise to the top of their school, who want their kids to have the corner office. They want their kids to be able to get the most prestigious positions.

I think in the minds of a lot of these people, not only now does their kid have to compete with all the other normal white kids in their community, they have to compete against the entire world. It’s a much larger anti-globalization backlash on the right, not only when it comes to things like immigration, but also trade and tariffs and restrictions like that.
When you talked to Indian Americans for this piece , what did you hear from them that surprised you?

Probably the most surprising thing was how much pragmatism they responded to all of this with. Nine times out of 10, when you have stories about racism, the victims of racism are outraged — understandably and justifiably outraged. Nobody wants to be mistreated. Nobody wants to be denigrated. They certainly don’t want to see restrictions on the right to immigration, or other things to limit their numbers, which is the end point of a lot of this.

At the same time, I think a lot of the people I spoke to were very upfront. They’re like, “Hey, look, we have found a lot of success in America. We got the golden ticket to be able to come here, for our kids to study here, to be able to really seek these opportunities, but we understand what’s happening in the economy. We understand there’s a lot of people who are struggling and then they see us rising to the top of all these organizations. They see us with our kind of well-ensconced place in the economy. And I think it’s important for us not to flaunt our success that much.” At least a couple people said something to that respect. They almost empathize with the people who were hating on them.

It struck me as such a classic immigrant pragmatism that you see from the first or second wave of immigrants: people who realize that they are newcomers to a society or maybe their parents were newcomers to a society, and that there is a certain level of grappling they have to do with, “Hey, how can we continue to have success? How can we continue to grind and resist this racism, but also not rub it in people’s faces that we’re doing well because the more they do that, the tougher it can be?”

A number brought up Vivek Ramaswamy in the sense that Vivek happened to go on social media and talk about what he felt like were deficiencies in American culture when it comes to studying, when it comes to working hard.

I think that in bringing that up, they were saying that that wasn’t particularly helpful because whatever positive aspects there may be to Indian immigrant culture, we shouldn’t talk about them in ways that denigrate other people because that’s obviously going to rub people the wrong way.

You’re making the point that some of the surge in anti-Indian racism on the right is about status anxiety. I was listening to this podcast that Chris Rufo and Jonathan Keeperman did. These are two influential right-wing activists. They called it “The Indian Question” — a lot of people’s eyebrows shot up — and they seem to be making the argument that it is about status anxiety.

They also were making less coherent arguments about how it’s un-American to study for the spelling bee, which is what South Asian kids do, and that white kids are more American because they play football, then they go to a party and get drunk, and then they get 1,500 on the SAT.
I’m not saying any of this makes sense. I’m saying it was fascinating. I’m assuming you watched that exchange. What did you make of that?

There’s a certain level of coping mechanism being deployed there in the sense that they are trying to explain the success of Indian Americans as a deficiency: “Maybe they’re getting to the top schools, but that’s because they’re shut in all day studying.”

But it’s not really true that Indian Americans are necessarily cloistered into unhealthy habits. They’re actually finding success across society. For instance, I’ve tutored kids for five, six years. I just really enjoy working with kids. And something you’ll find with a lot of the Indian American kids, they are actually getting increasingly well-rounded.

Part of that is because you have to, to have success, to get college admissions and so on and so forth. They almost always play sports. They’re involved in extracurriculars. You’re seeing a lot more Indian Americans go into the arts, into cultural fields, into Hollywood. I think that’s actually a very normal path for immigrants.

I think the first or second wave of immigrants has to be very pragmatic. They have to keep their heads down. They have to grind, study, and their parents encourage them to do the same thing. Indian American parents are always like, “You got to be a doctor. You got to be an engineer. Don’t be foolish and try to be a journalist or go to Hollywood.”

But as they establish themselves, as they build nest eggs, they have a little more breathing room, and so they can do different things. I know that Christopher Rufo, for instance, is an Italian American, and I believe I read one time that he even speaks Italian at home because he really values that culture so much and he wants to raise his kids in that. The first wave of Italian immigrants were no different than that. They cloistered into a few sectors where they felt they could find success that was necessary for their integration into the economy and to get their footing. But now we don’t think of Italian Americans as stereotyped into just a few parts of the country or a few parts of society — we barely notice, unless maybe you notice from someone’s name that there even are Italian Americans.

What they’re describing about Indian Americans is very normal. It’s actually very normal for first waves of immigrants to cluster in a few areas and then they spread themselves out as they’re able to get that a little bit of breathing room and room to ground to stand on.
